tldr: The authors theoretically prove that BayesDiff, an existing method for estimating the uncertainty of flow matching policies at test time, suffers from "variance collapse," where its variance decays to zero as numerical integration steps increase. To resolve this, they propose CoMP, a new method that tracks and propagates the cross-covariance between state and weights. CoMP achieves step-independent, accurate epistemic uncertainty estimation, improving failure detection and data collection efficiency.

As the step count increases, the total variance of BayesDiff decays at rate $O(1/T)$, collapsing the estimated uncertainty to zero (b, d). By tracking the cross-covariance between state and weights, the proposed CoMP (EKF/UKF) accurately recovers the true uncertainty (ground truth) regardless of the number of steps (c, d).
overview:
Flow matching and diffusion models have demonstrated impressive performance in recent robot policies (such as VLAs). However, they lack a mechanism to assess how unsure they are about their own outputs (epistemic uncertainty). Knowing this uncertainty is essential for robots to safely stop or collect additional training data when encountering novel situations. Yet, propagating weight uncertainty through the process of integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE) to generate actions is extremely difficult. Maintaining an ensemble of multiple models is impractical for massive foundation models due to computational and memory costs.

This led to interest in moment propagation methods like BayesDiff, which apply a last-layer Laplace approximation to a pre-trained model and pass the mean and covariance along the sampling trajectory. However, this paper mathematically proves that BayesDiff suffers from a critical flaw called "variance collapse": its estimated variance decays inversely with the number of Euler steps $T$ at rate $O(1/T)$, meaning the uncertainty vanishes toward zero as numerical integration accuracy improves.

The root cause of this collapse is that BayesDiff marginalizes out weights independently at each step, discarding the historical dependence that the current state was generated by past weights. To address this, the authors introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), which combines state and weight perturbations to maintain and propagate their cross-covariance. Derived as two update recursions inspired by the extended Kalman filter (EKF) and unscented Kalman filter (UKF), CoMP achieves theoretical consistency independent of the integration step count. Furthermore, by widening the last layer with vision-language observation embeddings already computed by the VLA, it dramatically improves sensitivity to ambiguous text prompts without retraining the model.

In experiments across simulation benchmarks (robomimic, LIBERO, and RoboLab), CoMP recovered nearly 100% of the true covariance and outperformed existing test-time uncertainty estimators in early detection of robot failures and efficient fine-tuning with limited demonstrations.
contributions: Theoretically proved that existing moment propagation methods such as BayesDiff suffer from $O(1/T)$ variance collapse in flow matching and diffusion ODEs.
Proposed CoMP (EKF and UKF variants), a new method that prevents variance collapse and estimates step-independent uncertainty by maintaining the cross-covariance between state and weights.

Introduced a technique to widen the last-layer Laplace posterior using existing observation embeddings without retraining or altering policy outputs, enhancing sensitivity to input ambiguities like language instructions.
Demonstrated on failure detection and demonstration selection benchmarks that CoMP matches deep ensemble performance at only a fraction of the cost of a single model.

sections.heading: Why do we need to measure the uncertainty of pre-trained robot policies?
sections.summary: Flow matching-based robot foundation models are powerful, but they cannot assess whether their predictions should be trusted in novel environments. While BayesDiff emerged as a low-cost, test-time method for measuring weight uncertainty, this paper reveals that it suffers from a fatal "variance collapse" where estimated variance vanishes as integration steps increase.
sections.details:
In recent years, flow matching has been widely adopted as the action generation head for state-of-the-art robot foundation models (VLAs), covering everything from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, in novel situations outside their training set, there is no way to measure whether predicted action commands can actually be trusted. Quantifying the uncertainty over model parameters—namely, epistemic uncertainty—is crucial for safe robot operation.

Typically, deep ensembles trained across multiple models are used to measure epistemic uncertainty. However, training and maintaining multiple large foundation models is cost-prohibitive. Consequently, moment propagation (BayesDiff), which applies a Laplace approximation to the last layer of a single pre-trained model and propagates the mean and variance through the denoising chain, attracted significant attention.

Yet, the authors discovered a startling phenomenon: in flow matching and diffusion ODE samplers, the upper bound of the total variance estimated by BayesDiff decays at rate $O(1/T)$ relative to the number of Euler steps $T$. This creates a self-defeating trade-off where taking finer integration steps to improve numerical accuracy causes the reported uncertainty to collapse to zero.

To resolve this issue, this paper proposes Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), a new framework that explicitly carries the cross-covariance between state and weights. Additionally, it introduces an approach that widens the last-layer Laplace representation using observation embeddings already computed by the foundation model.

In contrast, the proposed CoMP (c) accurately recovers 99–100% of the true variance, remaining stable regardless of the number of steps.

sections.heading: Basics of flow matching policies and moment propagation
sections.summary: This section reviews action generation via flow matching, the Laplace approximation modeling posteriors as Gaussians, and BayesDiff update recursions. It highlights how BayesDiff marginalizes out weights at each step, ignoring the history-dependent nature of the generation process.
sections.details:
Let us review the foundational techniques underpinning this work.

### Action generation with flow matching
Flow matching learns a velocity field $u_\theta(x, t)$ that maps a noise distribution $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ to a target data distribution $x_1$. In robot policies, conditioned on an observation context $o$ (such as camera images and text prompts), an action chunk $x \in \mathbb{R}^{D}$ ($D = H \times d_a$) spanning $H$ future steps is generated all at once from noise via numerical ODE integration. With Euler integration using step size $\Delta t = 1/T$, the update $x_{i+1} = x_i + \Delta t \, u_\theta(x_i, t_i)$ is repeated $T$ times.

### Laplace approximation and last-layer widening
The model's weight posterior $p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})$ is approximated as a Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}, \Sigma_\theta)$ around the MAP estimate using the Hessian (curvature) of the loss function. Since computing the full Hessian across all parameters is too expensive, it is typically restricted to the last-layer weights. However, relying solely on the last layer risks feature collapse, prompting prior work like LULA to widen hidden layer features without altering model outputs.

### BayesDiff update recursions and their blind spot
BayesDiff propagates the state mean $m_i$ and coordinate-wise variance $P_i$ (diagonal elements only) along integration steps. However, its expectation calculation relies on the predictive distribution $p(u \mid x_i, t_i, \mathcal{D})$ by marginalizing out weights $\theta$ at each step. This effectively assumes that weights are redrawn independently at every step. In reality, the exact same weights $\theta$ are used from the start to the end of sampling, and state $x_i$ itself is strongly shaped by those weights. Discarding this dependency is the root cause of variance collapse.

sections.heading: Uncovering the variance collapse mechanism and the CoMP algorithm
sections.summary: The authors prove a theorem showing that BayesDiff's total variance decays to zero at rate $O(1/T)$, then derive CoMP based on a linearized model combining state and weight perturbations. They provide two implementations (EKF and UKF) alongside a head-widening method using internal VLA embeddings.
sections.details:
### Theoretical proof of variance collapse
Under standard assumptions of Lipschitz continuity for the velocity field and bounded predictive variance, tracking the total variance $\operatorname{tr} P_T$ in BayesDiff reveals that uncertainty injected at each step scales as $\Delta t^2 = 1/T^2$. Summing this over $T$ steps results in $\operatorname{tr} P_T \le e^{2L} \bar{\sigma}_{\max}^2 / T$, proving that variance collapses completely to zero as $T \to \infty$. Increasing Euler steps $T$ to improve numerical integration accuracy paradoxically destroys the uncertainty.

### Deriving CoMP by tracking cross-covariance
To fix this fundamental problem, CoMP avoids premature weight marginalization and linearizes state perturbations $\delta x_i$ and weight perturbations $\delta \theta$ simultaneously around the mean trajectory. Forming a joint vector $z_i = (\delta x_i, \delta \theta)$ allows Euler updates to be expressed in closed form as linear mappings via block matrices. This yields update recursions that propagate three quantities concurrently:
- State mean $m_i$: tracks the MAP trajectory
- State covariance $P_i$: the spread of the state
- State-weight cross-covariance $C_i = \mathrm{Cov}(\delta x_i, \delta \theta)$: the history of how state deviations were induced by weights

By preserving $C_i$, step-wise contributions accumulate as amplitudes rather than squared sums, mathematically guaranteeing an upper bound on total variance that converges to an $O(1)$ constant independent of $T$.

### Two implementations (EKF and UKF) and head widening
- **CoMP-EKF**: Computes state Jacobians via autodiff through the action expert and updates them as extended Kalman filter prediction steps.
- **CoMP-UKF**: Uses the unscented transform with sigma points passed through nonlinear maps. This avoids EKF local linearization errors and captures nonlinear dynamics.
- **Head widening via observation embeddings**: Unlike LULA, which requires gathering OOD data, this approach adds latent features $c(o)$ generated by a pre-trained VLA (such as $\pi_{0.5}$ or SmolVLA) from images and text into the last-layer input. Initializing added weights to zero enhances uncertainty estimation expressiveness without altering the original policy's predictions by a single millimeter.

sections.heading: Benchmark experiments: Covariance fidelity, prompt ambiguity, failure detection, and fine-tuning
sections.summary: Using three robot policies and three manipulation benchmarks, the authors evaluated four questions. CoMP recovered true covariance with over 99% accuracy, responded reliably to prompt ambiguity, and outperformed baselines in failure detection and demonstration selection.
sections.details:
### Q1: Does propagated covariance match the true posterior?
On three robomimic tasks (Lift, PickPlaceCan, NutAssemblySquare), CoMP was compared against an ensemble of 4,000 trajectories sampled from the posterior (ground truth $P^\star$). BayesDiff recovered only 6% to 23% of the true variance, remaining severely underestimated even when tracking full covariance matrices. In contrast, CoMP recovered the true distribution with less than 0.2% error in total variance ratio and under 10% error in correlation structure (variogram divergence).

### Q2: Does the widened head respond to language prompt ambiguity?
Across 10 RoboLab tasks, estimated uncertainty was evaluated for identical initial states under three prompt variants: specific, standard, and ambiguous (Figure F8). With standard heads, all methods produced nearly constant uncertainty, ignoring prompt differences. With the widened head using observation embeddings, uncertainty rose sharply as prompts became more ambiguous. Furthermore, while BayesDiff lost sensitivity as integration steps increased, CoMP maintained high, consistent sensitivity.

### Q3: Can runtime execution failures be detected early?
Using conformal prediction, early failure detection was tested in perturbed robomimic environments (perturbed initial poses, Figure F11) and nine LIBERO-90 tasks (Figure F12). CoMP-UKF matched the best baseline on robomimic and ranked first among test-time estimators on LIBERO-90 across accuracy (0.794), time-weighted accuracy (TWA 0.643), and detection time (DT 0.474). It approached deep ensemble performance while requiring the memory of only a single model and under 1% additional parameters.

### Q4: Does uncertainty-based demonstration selection improve fine-tuning?
For task adaptation on LIBERO-10 using SmolVLA (Figure F13), demonstrations were selected under budget constraints $X$ (25 to 250) based on highest uncertainty. CoMP-UKF achieved an average +3.5 point success rate gain over random sampling, outperforming a two-model VFD ensemble (1.2GB) with a single model and just a 75MB posterior file. When step count grew from 10 to 50, BayesDiff's improvement plummeted from +2.7 to -2.9 points, whereas CoMP-UKF remained steady at +3.3 to +3.7 points.

sections.heading: Related work and positioning of this paper
sections.summary: This section situates CoMP within the broader landscape of machine learning uncertainty estimation (ensembles and Bayesian approaches), moment propagation in diffusion models, and robotics applications like failure detection and active learning.
sections.details:
Quantifying epistemic uncertainty has long been studied to ensure model reliability. While deep ensembles and Bayesian neural networks are prominent paradigms, compute and storage overheads become major bottlenecks for large foundation models. In diffusion and flow matching models, methods such as trajectory divergence mutual information (DECU) or velocity field disagreement integration (VFD) have been proposed, but they often still rely on multiple models or repeated sampling.

Moment propagation (BayesDiff) was a promising framework for efficiently passing variance from a single model posterior, yet as demonstrated in this work, it suffered from variance collapse. CoMP overcomes this theoretical defect for the first time by recovering the cross-covariance between state and weights.

In robotics applications, uncertainty plays a vital role in runtime monitoring, active learning, and data-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., SAVE, CUPID). CoMP provides a highly accurate, post-hoc tool to support these downstream tasks without requiring model retraining.

sections.heading: Limitations of CoMP and future directions
sections.summary: Identified constraints include requiring a linear final layer to obtain analytic weight Jacobians, alongside increased inference runtime and memory consumption that scale with action chunk dimension $D$.
sections.details:
Despite its strong capabilities, CoMP exhibits several clear limitations in practical deployment:

- **Dependence on a linear last layer**: To compute Jacobians with respect to weights analytically, the architecture must assume a linear final layer. Extending the Laplace approximation deeper into the network remains computationally difficult.
- **Computational cost scaling with output dimension $D$**: As the product of action chunk horizon and action degrees of freedom ($D = H \times d_a$) grows, the computational burden increases. CoMP-UKF evaluates $2D+1$ sigma points per step, while CoMP-EKF requires $D$ backpropagation passes.
- **Inference speed trade-offs**: On $\pi_{0.5}$ ($D=70$), CoMP-UKF requires 1.85 seconds per decision, but on SmolVLA with longer chunks ($D=350$), it consumes 3.38 seconds and 4.6GB of peak memory. While entirely suitable for offline demonstration selection, integrating it into high-frequency, real-time control loops will require lightweight adaptations like low-rank covariance approximations.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: By revealing variance collapse in conventional moment propagation for flow matching policies, CoMP and embedding-widened heads pave the way for extracting high-quality uncertainty from a single model.
sections.details: This work proposed CoMP, an epistemic uncertainty estimation framework for pre-trained flow matching robot policies. It uncovered the theoretical mechanism behind BayesDiff's variance collapse—where refining numerical integration drives uncertainty to zero—and resolved it by modeling state-weight cross-covariance. In addition, widening the policy head using internal VLA observation embeddings enables sensitivity to prompt ambiguity without retraining. This constitutes a highly practical foundation for robots to recognize their own limits, operate safely, and learn efficiently.

takeaways: Existing moment propagation methods like BayesDiff suffer from "variance collapse," where estimated variance decays at $O(1/T)$ as ODE solver steps increase.
Propagating the cross-covariance between state and weights alongside moments recovers theoretically consistent uncertainty estimates that do not depend on the step count.
Widening the final layer with vision-language embeddings already computed by VLAs substantially boosts sensitivity to instruction ambiguity without changing policy outputs.
Applying a Laplace approximation and CoMP to a single pre-trained model matches or beats deep ensembles on failure detection and data selection at a fraction of the cost.
limitations: When action chunk dimension $D$ is large, UKF sigma point evaluations and EKF Jacobian backprop passes increase, resulting in inference latencies of several seconds that require optimization for real-time control.
Relies on a structural requirement that the final network layer is linear to allow analytic parameter differentiation.
Covariance matrix memory scales as $D \times D$, necessitating extensions like low-rank approximations when applied to high-dimensional whole-body control or very long prediction horizons.
